title: Bonaventure's journey
hookLine: the Franciscan who saw every creature as a step toward God

lines: UP THE MOUNTAIN OF LA VERNA.
cards: What would it take to see a sparrow as a staircase? A Franciscan friar named Bonaventure climbs a mountain in Italy called La Verna.

It's where, the story goes, Francis had a vision near the end of his life: a fiery angel, a seraph, with six wings. Bonaventure has a heavy job by now: he leads the whole family of Franciscan brothers.
He goes up, he says, looking for peace. And while he's there, thinking about Francis's vision, an idea comes that becomes a small book.

teach.b: The book is called The Journey of the Mind into God. Bonaventure reads the six wings as six steps. The soul climbs, he says, like going up a ladder, and the first rungs are right under your feet: the things God made.
A stone, a river, a sparrow.

Each carries a trace of the one who made it, the way a footprint in the sand tells you someone walked there. Then you climb inward, to your own mind, where he finds God's image. Then upward, beyond what the mind can hold.

teach.h: SEEN BY THE THINGS THAT ARE MADE.
teach.b: Behind that is a line from Romans, in the King James Bible: "For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made."

Francis is close behind it, the man whose song made the sun a brother. Bonaventure gives that love a map. Every creature is a step: not a stopping place, not something to grab, but a step on the way up.
By the stories told about him, he was a humble climber.

teach.h: HANG THE HAT ON A TREE.
teach.b: Tradition says that when messengers came to tell him the pope had made him a cardinal, they found him washing dishes, and he asked them to hang the cardinal's hat on a tree until he finished.
Whether or not it went that way, it's the kind of story told about a man who saw holy things in ordinary places. A dish. A tree.

how: Franciscans and other Christians read Bonaventure's Journey of the Mind into God slowly, often on retreat, and some practice prayerful walks in nature that follow its first steps.

o: a pilgrimage on foot to the tomb of Francis
a crusader's voyage to see the Holy Land
climbing toward God through the things he made

p: a trace of the one who made it

s: Bonaventure says the climb to God starts by turning away from creatures
it starts with them: the first steps are the things God made.
Bonaventure reads the seraph's six wings as six steps
the soul climbs like a ladder: outward, inward, then upward.
Bonaventure was a Dominican like Aquinas
he was a Franciscan, and led the Franciscan brothers.

games.q: you're Bonaventure, up to your elbows in dishwater. messengers arrive to say the pope has made you a cardinal, and they hand you the hat. what do you do?
o: dry your hands and put the hat on at once.
ask them to hang it on a tree until you finish the dishes.
refuse the hat and send them away.
games.why: tradition says he asked them to hang the hat on a tree until the dishes were done.

practice: Find one living thing you can see from where you are, a plant, a bird outside, even your own hand, and look at it as if it were the first of its kind you'd ever seen.
Then let your attention rise a little, past it, toward whatever made it, however you name that. If you pray, give thanks for this one creature; if not, let the looking be thanks enough.

wordCard.voice: Bonaventure's journey. His book The Journey of the Mind into God: climbing from the things God made, inward to the mind, and upward to God.

orig.note: Latin: the journey of the mind into God, the title of Bonaventure's book.

carryVoice: Your line: every creature a step. Not a stopping place, but a rung. Step by step, day eight hundred twenty-three.

sources.ref: Bonaventure, The Journey of the Mind into God, prologue and chapters 1–2
